subject: literature
passage: Charles Dickens first ended Great Expectations (1861) with Pip and Estella meeting briefly and parting for good. When his friend, the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton, urged a happier conclusion, Dickens rewrote the final scene so that the two leave the ruined garden together. Many critics see this revision as a betrayal of the novel's sad, clear-eyed logic.
passage_b: The published ending is far less cheerful than its reputation suggests. Pip and Estella meet as two people worn down by years of disappointment, and the closing words, "I saw no shadow of another parting from her," are strangely hesitant; they describe what Pip did not see rather than what will happen. Read closely, the revised ending keeps the novel's somber tone and leaves the couple's future uncertain.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' view of the revised ending in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that Dickens never wrote any ending other than the published one
choices.B: By suggesting that Bulwer-Lytton wrote the final scene of the novel himself
choices.C: By arguing that the revised ending is more uncertain and somber than critics suggest
choices.D: By agreeing that the revision gives the novel a simple, happy conclusion

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that critics see the revised ending as a happy betrayal of the novel's "sad, clear-eyed logic." Text 2 says the ending is "far less cheerful than its reputation suggests": the final words are "strangely hesitant," and the ending "keeps the novel's somber tone." So Text 2 would say the revision does not betray the novel's mood.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses only the published ending and never denies that Dickens first wrote a different one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 says Bulwer-Lytton urged a change and Dickens rewrote the scene; neither text says Bulwer-Lytton wrote it.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 points to the worn-down characters and the hesitant final words to show that the ending stays somber.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that the ending only seems happy; read closely, it is somber and uncertain.
